passage: In my first month of college, the hostel's first-year group chat became a place where seniors posted my photos with captions about my 'village English' and my oiled hair. Every day, a new one. When I finally wrote 'please stop', a senior replied, 'Relax, it's just ragging, it's fun, everyone goes through it.' I believed that for a while. I told myself I was too sensitive. I stopped eating in the mess. Then Himani, my roommate, read the chat over my shoulder and said, 'Sarita, this isn't fun. They're humiliating you every day.' Hearing it named plainly was like breathing again. She walked with me to the warden that same evening. The warden listened, said none of it was my fault, and called the anti-ragging committee before we left the office. It stopped within a week.

qa.q: What did the senior reply when Sarita wrote 'please stop'?
qa.a: The senior replied, 'Relax, it's just ragging, it's fun, everyone goes through it.'

qa.q: Why did Sarita start to believe that the problem was being too sensitive?
qa.a: The label 'just ragging' made the daily mockery sound normal, so Sarita's real hurt began to look like the problem instead of what the seniors were doing.

qa.q: What choice by Himani changed things, and why?
qa.a: Himani named it plainly as humiliation and walked Sarita to the warden that same evening, which turned private pain into something adults could act on.

qa.q: How did the warden respond, and why did it matter to Sarita?
qa.a: The warden listened, said none of it was Sarita's fault and called the anti-ragging committee at once, which showed that Sarita was believed and protected.

grounding: Shows a first-year student mocked daily in a group chat who is told it is only ragging, until a roommate names it plainly and the warden acts the same evening.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college counselling cell, Monday
Neelam, first-year B.Sc., came in at 4 p.m. and showed me her phone. For three weeks her class group chat has been posting edited pictures of her with an animal's face, and voice notes copying her stammer. When she complained, the group admin wrote, 'It's just fun, bro. Don't be so serious.' She said to me, 'Maybe I can't take a joke.' Her hands shook while she scrolled. I told her plainly that this is mockery, not fun, that it is not her fault, and that she was right to come. With her permission I took screenshots and reported it to the anti-ragging committee and the head of department before six this evening. I've arranged for a senior mentor to sit with her in class, and her parents know. I'll see her again tomorrow at lunch.
Swati

qa.q: What did the group admin write when Neelam complained?
qa.a: The admin wrote, 'It's just fun, bro. Don't be so serious.'

qa.q: Why did Neelam say 'Maybe I can't take a joke'?
qa.a: Being told it was 'just fun' made Neelam doubt her own hurt, so she blamed herself instead of the people mocking her.

qa.q: Which of Swati's steps matters most, and why?
qa.a: Calling it mockery and saying it wasn't Neelam's fault gives her distress its real name, and reporting it the same day makes sure it actually stops.

qa.q: How might the group admin see the chat differently from Neelam?
qa.a: The admin sees harmless fun from the outside, while for Neelam each edited picture and voice note has meant three weeks of dread and shaking hands.

grounding: Shows a counsellor's note on a student mocked in a class group chat and told it was just fun, who names it plainly and reports it the same day.

passage:
Wednesday night
Today the seniors' group posted my photo again, the one from orientation where I tripped, with 'Miss Circus' written over it. Forty-two laughing reactions. When I asked one of them to take it down, she said, 'It's just ragging, yaar. It's how we bond.' It doesn't feel like bonding. It feels like I can't walk into the canteen. I cried in the washroom before lab.
Vikas saw my face and asked. I showed him. He didn't say 'ignore it'. He said, 'That's bullying, Sunaina. Calling it ragging doesn't make it okay.' He came with me to the warden's office after lab. Warden ma'am read every post, said it was not my fault, and phoned the anti-ragging committee right there. The photo was gone by 9 p.m.
I'm still shaky. But someone called it by its real name.

qa.a: It shows that Sunaina's real experience, dreading the canteen and crying before lab, doesn't match the friendly label, which was trying to erase that hurt.

passage: I'm Dilnaz, and I sat next to Zeenat at Friday's town hall. The new director clicked through slides about 'rightsizing for agility' and 'releasing talent to the market'. People nodded. Zeenat raised her hand. 'Sorry, I just want to understand. Rightsizing means how many people lose their jobs, and in which teams?' The room went quiet. The director said, 'We're optimising roles.' Zeenat said, calmly, 'So, people. How many, and when will they be told?' After a long pause he said, 'About forty, mostly in support. Next month.' I saw the support team's faces at the back. Afterwards three of them came up and thanked her. I don't know what she felt, standing up like that. Her voice didn't shake. But when she sat down, her hand held the edge of her chair very tightly.

qa.q: How many people did the director say would be affected?
qa.a: The director said about forty, mostly in support.

qa.q: What might Zeenat's tight grip on the chair suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was nervous about speaking up even though her voice stayed calm; she cared enough about the people affected to do it anyway.

qa.q: Why was Zeenat's question so effective?
qa.a: Asking how many people, which teams and when turned soft words like 'rightsizing' into plain facts about real people, which the room could no longer look past.

qa.q: How might the support team at the back have felt after the question?
qa.a: The support team probably felt shaken but respected, since they finally heard what 'rightsizing' meant for them, which is why three came to thank Zeenat.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, an adult who hears a layoff called rightsizing and asks plainly what happens to whom.

passage: Mehak, when the HR note said 'transition support for impacted resources', you frowned, and I liked that. Let me tell you why. Twenty years ago, at the textile mill office, I sat in a meeting where the owner's son called closing the dyeing unit 'streamlining'. Everyone clapped politely. I, Disha, was twenty-five and scared, but I asked, 'Streamlining means Mohan-bhai, Salim, the twelve dyers. What happens to them?' He didn't like it. But the word stopped working. Once we said their names, the meeting had to talk about notice, about wages, about moving some to the new unit. Eight of the twelve kept jobs. So when you see 'impacted resources', ask which people. Say their names out loud. It's the smallest thing you can do, and sometimes it's enough.

qa.a: Eight of the twelve kept jobs.

qa.a: Saying their names turned 'streamlining' into real people losing work, so the meeting had to discuss notice, wages and moves instead of hiding behind a soft word.

qa.q: How might the dyers have fared if nobody had asked?
qa.a: They might have learned of the closure with no notice or plan, their lives hidden behind 'streamlining'; being named gave eight of them a way to stay.

passage: In the Class 4 lunch hall of the school in Darjeeling, the girls had a rule this week: nobody sits with Rinku. Dolma didn't start it. But when Rinku came towards their bench with her tiffin, Dolma moved her bag onto the empty space, like everyone else. Rinku stood there, then went and sat on the steps alone. Anirban sir had seen it from the corridor. After lunch he called Dolma to the staff room. 'Why did you put your bag there?' Dolma twisted her plait. 'Everyone was doing it, sir. It wasn't just me.' 'How many bags were on the bench?' 'Six.' 'And whose bag was on Rinku's place?' Dolma looked at her shoes. 'Mine.' 'So one of the six was you.' Her eyes filled. 'Tomorrow,' Anirban sir said, 'you can choose again.'

qa.a: 'Whose bag was on Rinku's place?' pointed Dolma to her own choice, so she could see that one of the six was her, not just 'everyone'.

qa.a: Rinku stood with her tiffin, found the bench blocked, and sat alone on the steps, likely feeling hurt and unwanted.

Mentor's note, second-year B.A., Thursday
Aditi came to see me after class. On Tuesday night the class meme page posted Manas's poem from the college magazine with mocking edits, and about sixty people piled in with comments. Aditi said she watched for an hour. 'I kept thinking someone else would say something. There were sixty of us.' Nobody did. At midnight she wrote one line: 'This is his real poem and he's in this group. Let's stop.' A few people agreed; the comments slowed and then stopped. Two people messaged her privately to say they had felt the same. Manas has not been to class since. I spoke with Manas today, told him none of this was his fault, and asked the page admins to remove the post. I've also informed the student welfare office. I told Aditi that one calm voice mattered.
Ishita

qa.q: How many people piled in with comments?
qa.a: About sixty people piled in with comments.

qa.a: With sixty people watching, Aditi assumed someone else would speak up, so the responsibility felt spread thin, even though she was uneasy.

qa.a: Manas saw his own poem mocked by dozens of classmates and hasn't come to class since, which shows how humiliating it was.

Subject: Batch 47 straps

Dear Chinmay,
I understand your instruction from this morning: ship Batch 47 of the cycle helmets on Friday and leave the strap test failures out of the report, because the client is waiting.
I've thought about it carefully, and I can't sign the report that way. Eleven of the forty sample straps failed the pull test. If I leave that out, it's still my name on the report and my choice, whatever I was told. I'd rather answer for raising it than for hiding it.
So I'm doing two things. I've copied this email to Ms Pillai in Quality, as our process requires for any failed test. And I'm free tomorrow to help find a replacement batch of straps quickly, so we lose as little time with the client as possible.
I know this makes Friday harder. I'm sorry for that part.
Thomas

qa.a: It shows Thomas sees the choice as Thomas's own, whatever the order, and would rather carry the discomfort of speaking up than the weight of hiding a safety problem.

qa.q: What made Thomas's way of raising it responsible rather than rebellious?
qa.a: Thomas acknowledged the instruction, followed the proper process by copying Quality, and offered practical help to limit the delay, so it was a correct channel, not a fight.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel reading this email?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel pressured and a bit exposed, but also aware that Thomas has offered a clear, respectful way to fix the problem before the helmets reach riders.

passage: The purifier seals, Madhuri. That's my answer to your question about the hardest week of my working life. I was twenty-four, in quality control at a factory making water purifiers. We found that a whole lot of seals leaked after a few weeks. My manager said, 'Just pass them. Most customers won't notice, and if they do, it's warranty. I'll take responsibility.' For a whole day I told myself that: he'll take responsibility. Then I thought, no, I'm the one stamping 'passed'. It's my stamp, Vandana's stamp. So I went to his cabin and said, 'I understand what you want. I still can't pass them.' He was angry. I wrote it up the way our quality manual says and sent it to the plant head. Two weeks later the lot was pulled back from the warehouse. My manager didn't talk to me for a month. I'd do it again.

passage: I'm Jeevan. I was on the same site as Anirban the day the contractor told him to plaster over the crack in the third-floor beam before the client inspection. 'Don't make it a story. I'll handle it,' the contractor said. I watched Anirban stand under that beam for a long time, looking up. Then he said, loudly enough for the crew to hear, 'I understand what you're asking. But if I sign the checklist, it's my signature, not yours.' He photographed the crack, wrote it in the site register with the time, and phoned the structural engineer from the gate. The contractor shouted. Anirban's hands were shaking; I could see that. But he didn't change the register. By evening the engineer had come, and work on the floor above was stopped for repairs. I don't know what it cost him inside. I just know I'd want him on my building.

passage: In Class 11 our school cricket team had a running joke about the boys from the Hill Road academy. We called them 'the cattle'. I, Dhruv, made up half the jokes: they moo instead of appealing, they need a farmer to set the field. It was easy to laugh, because they weren't really people to us, just a colour of jersey. Then at the district camp I was paired with Manoj from Hill Road for fielding drills. He was funny. He carried spare grips for everyone. On the last day he said, 'You're the one who does the cattle jokes, right? My little brother cried about that video.' I didn't know what to say. That's when I understood how the jokes had worked: as long as they had no faces, I didn't have to feel anything. I stopped making them. I still think about his brother.

qa.a: Getting to know Manoj, and hearing that his little brother cried over a video, gave the group real faces, and Dhruv stopped making the jokes.

qa.a: Manoj may have felt hurt on his brother's behalf and a bit wary, but chose to say it calmly after days of friendly drills.
